candidato.resumo: Like cholesterol, inflammation causally contributes to the risk of cardiovascular disease, but findings from the clinical trial ZEUS indicate that the road to targeting inflammation may be less straightforward than once thought. texto_fonte:
Heart researchers unpack neutral findings from ZEUS, an anti-inflammatory clinical trial
Like cholesterol, inflammation causally contributes to the risk of cardiovascular disease, but findings from the clinical trial ZEUS indicate that the road to targeting inflammation may be less straightforward than once thought. ZEUS, a global phase 3 clinical trial led by Mass General Brigham researcher Paul Ridker, M.D., tested a drug that targets interleukin-6 (IL-6), a downstream inflammatory molecule. IL-6 inhibitors are commonly used to treat autoimmune disorders. However, while the new drug known as ziltivekimab lowered IL-6 levels, it did not reduce cardiovascular event rates compared to placebo.
In a late-breaking clinical trial presentation at the American Heart Association Scientific Session and in a simultaneous publication in New England Journal of Medicine, Ridker and colleagues detail the findings and lay out several potential explanations, including differences between the population enrolled in ZEUS and those enrolled in previous trials and the difference between IL-6 and other inflammation targets.
"The findings from ZEUS illustrate why clinical trials are so important: We don't yet have all of the answers and science is often about trial and error," said Ridker. "We already know from prior studies that targeting inflammation can reduce rates of heart attack and stroke. The critical question is which drug works best in which patients."
Testing a different inflammatory target
Previous work in the Canakinumab Anti-inflammatory Thrombosis Outcomes Study (CANTOS), also led by Ridker, showed that targeting a midstream interleukin known as IL-1b significantly lowered rates of recurrent heart attacks and strokes. In ZEUS, researchers tested ziltivekimab, a monoclonal antibody that targets a similar pathway but downstream at the level of IL-6.
"Given our neutral findings, one logical next step is to move upstream, instead of downstream, to find the right target," said Ridker. "For example, there are multiple new agents in development that can inhibit the upstream NLRP3 inflammasome. At the same time, it remains quite possible that downstream IL-6 inhibition is in fact effective, but that ZEUS targeted the wrong patient population."
Advanced disease may limit benefit
Like CANTOS, ZEUS enrolled people with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and systemic inflammation. But unlike CANTOS, ZEUS participants were a decade older, had significant kidney disease and often had longstanding diabetes and heart failure.
"In people with nonmodifiable disease, the horse may already have been out of the barn," Ridker said, noting that other ongoing and planned trials of IL-6 inhibition are focused instead on modifiable earlier-stage disease.
In the Ziltivekimab Cardiovascular Outcomes Study (ZEUS), researchers did not see a statistically significant difference in the rate of a combination of heart attack, stroke or cardiovascular death (the primary endpoint occurred in 561 participants in the treatment group compared to 565 in the placebo group). Safety was reassuring, with no adverse effect on total mortality, though a small increase in rates of infection was observed.
Proven options remain underused
The authors conclude that further trials are needed to understand how and in whom anti-inflammatory therapy can be given to reduce cardiovascular event rates. But they also note that for patients with stable atherosclerotic disease, the LoDoCo2 and COLCOT trials have already shown that the generic drug colchicine—which is also an anti-inflammatory medication—significantly reduces risk of cardiovascular events. Low-dose colchicine is approved by the U.S. FDA for use as an anti-inflammatory drug to lower rates of heart attack and stroke.
"What ZEUS shows us is that this particular drug in this particular setting didn't work," said Ridker. "But it's important to remember that we have other proven anti-inflammatory drugs such as low-dose colchicine that are being underutilized today in our patients with stable atherosclerosis. The results of ZEUS, taken together with the results of our other studies, help point us where we should go next."
Ridker points out that part of that direction should be quality preventive care; diet, exercise and smoking cessation all reduce inflammation and all lower cardiac risks, while other common drugs including statins and GLP-1 receptor agonists like semaglutide and tirzepatide also have important anti-inflammatory properties.
"Doctors will not treat what they do not measure," Ridker said, noting that a recent American College of Cardiology scientific statement called for broad screening for high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), an inexpensive blood test indicating substantial inflammatory risk.
Publication details
Interleukin-6 Inhibition with Ziltivekimab for Atherosclerotic Disease, New England Journal of Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.1056/NEJMoa2612126
Journal information: New England Journal of Medicine

candidato.titulo: The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.
candidato.resumo: Genes and archaeology are revealing how Bantu speakers spread across much of Africa.

texto_fonte:
It’s not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between 1000 to 1700 AD—were masters.
At sites near the city’s stone ruins, clusters of iron-smelting furnaces survive today as mounds of rubble. At Mashava, a village 25 miles northwest, fragments bear fingermarks of those who long ago smoothed the structures’ clay interiors.
Some of the furnaces were nearly an adult’s arm span in width, with walls thick and strong to contain the heat of more than 2,100° Fahrenheit needed to smelt iron. Unlike other furnaces that required workers to force air into them with bellows, these were designed to suck air in, then out through a chimney, no human labor required. This would have made it significantly easier to produce the iron, which was fashioned into hoes, axes, and arrowheads.
“The number and size of these furnaces, together with the use of natural-draft technology, indicate intensive and technologically sophisticated iron production,” says archaeometallurgist Ezekiel Mtetwa of Chicago’s Field Museum of Natural History, who has long studied the furnaces.
Scientists are extremely interested in the peoples who created this and other iron-powered societies across eastern and southern Africa. Research points to an adaptable and innovative group from western Africa as the masterminds. Known as Bantu speakers, these communities began gradually expanding across the continent’s southern half, starting from 6,000 to 4,000 years ago. In doing so, they introduced a fundamentally new, sedentary way of life—characterized by farming, raising livestock, pottery-making, and metalworking—to regions previously dominated by hunter-gatherer communities.
This migration transformed not only the region’s history and technology, but also its languages: Today, around 350 million Africans speak one of roughly 500 distinct Bantu tongues, from southern African Zulu to eastern African Swahili. And at least as many Africans—as well as many African Americans and Afro-Latinos—carry Bantu ancestry in their DNA.

This is such a novel and underrated form factor for a household robot. I absolutely love it.

[ Agility Robotics ]
Happy Halloween from Flexiv Robotics!
Okay WHAT.
[ Flexiv ]
Nothing hides from SCUTL. Not even the paranormal.
Thanks, Dan!
Happy Halloween from HEBI Robotics!
We asked ourselves if you can carve a pumpkin using nothing but a T-Series arm and a drill originally designed to run an auger. The answer is yes, so long as you don’t care too much about accuracy. Basic pathing commands running off a laptop, stability provided by a quick connection to Treadward. Happy Halloween, HEBI fans!
[ HEBI ]
Something strange has been happening at KIMLAB. Our snacks kept disappearing… and we finally caught the culprit. Meet GG, our new lab friend. GG is a character robot inspired by the Ggeomeoksali from Netflix’s “The East Palace.” GG sneaks around for snacks, eats them, sleeps most of the time, begs everyone for more food, and leans on whoever is nearby. Cute, comforting, and a good friend. But GG is still a gwi-mae… so who knows what else it can do.
[ Kinetic Intelligent Machine Lab ]
Happy Halloween from Dusty Robotics!
[ Dusty ]
Finally, a robot with a butt.
[ JSK Lab ]
Thanks, Shunnosuke!
Any drone can crash into a tree once. This drone can crash into a tree MORE than once.
[ ETH Zurich ]
Lume is a robotic floor lamp that moves around your home, helps with everyday chores, and returns to being a beautiful lamp when it’s done.
[ Syncere ]
If we’re going to use robots at work or at home, they’re going to have to communicate with us. At Toyota Research Institute, a team of robotics user experience designers is working on the sounds, gestures, light patterns, and interfaces that allow robots to let us know that they are on the move, that we need to stay clear, or to tell us that they just really need help. Steffi Paepcke, Director of Robotics User Experience at TRI, accepts the challenge to explain how her team approaches this work in just one minute.
I need a sound for when people around me need to give me space.
The entirely student-run, self-taught and highly collaborative MIT Combat Robotics Club (CRC) builds high-energy fighting machines to compete in House Battles and larger competitions. Fans of the hit show BattleBots may remember some of CRC’s past robots, including Uppercut, SawBlaze, the Dentist, and Overhaul. CRC is open to every MIT student regardless of year, major, or prior experience. Students learn a variety of skills, from CAD and FEA to CNC Machining and Welding—and they learn through watching their creations get completely destroyed.
Happy birthday, JPL!
Where do I get a shirt like that last guy has?
[ JPL ]
Can machines be creative? In this first episode of Moonshot, host Mike Massimino talks with Hod Lipson, a Columbia Engineering roboticist whose work includes robots that learn and adapt. Lipson, the James and Sally Scapa Professor of Innovation in Columbia’s Department of Mechanical Engineering, explains why physical AI is so difficult, how engineers and AI might work together on new designs, and how he defines creativity. He also shares advice on why playing it safe can limit your impact.
This closing fireside chat brings together two of the field’s most consequential builders—Jeff Dean, whose work at Google has helped define the modern AI stack, and Fei-Fei Li, whose case for human-centered AI has shaped how the field thinks about who this technology should actually serve. Coming at the end of a day spent grappling with AI’s risks and unresolved questions, the conversation turns to where the two of them agree, where they don’t, and what they think the choices ahead really come down to.

candidato.titulo: How Grab Improved Mobile App Stability by Safely Handling Surge in AI-Generated Code Changes
candidato.resumo: The growing adoption of AI coding assistants has accelerated development and increased the volume of code changes per release, bringing more opportunities for defects and crashes, says Grab. To address these challenges, they implemented a layered defense strategy to prevent, detect, and contain crashes throughout the development and release lifecycle. By Sergio De Simone

texto_fonte:
The growing adoption of AI coding assistants has accelerated development and increased the volume of code changes per release, bringing more opportunities for defects and crashes, says Grab. To address these challenges, they implemented a layered defense strategy to prevent, detect, and contain crashes throughout the development and release lifecycle.
Grab observes that "AI is speeding up how fast code is written; the layered defense is what makes that speed safe":
At [Grab's] scale, crashes leaking into production are an ongoing risk. A high volume of merge requests lands every week across many product teams, many shipping features behind flags that are switched on independently of releases. Any one of those changes can introduce a crash.
Beyond degrading the user's experience, a mobile app's crash reduces crash-free session rates and, as a consequence, the app's Google Play ranking. It also has an increased cost because not all users enable automatic updates, meaning that "a mobile crash that ships stays on users' devices" for longer. Furthermore, not all crashes come with clean, symbolicated stack trace, which means that "finding the cause means cross-referencing release timelines, flag rollouts, and session metadata".
Grab's layered defense follows a shift-left strategy aimed at catching crashes as early as possible through a series of safeguards along the development cycle phases: pre-merge through pre-production, release control, and post-release response.
During the pre-merge to pre-production phase, the goal is prevention, which Grab describes as its "primary line of defense". To achieve this, Grab engineers use static code analyzers such as Android Lint and SwiftLint to catch issues before code even merges via platform-specific, community-based, and custom lint rules; automated and manual testing, including unit tests, UI tests, and quality assurance (QA) checks; and Grab Early Access (GEA), a pre-production gate where early builds are distributed to internal users and actively monitored for crashes:
A crash that only a handful of internal users see in GEA would, at production scale, translate into a substantial spike in the crash rate, extra support load, and potentially a hotfix. Catching these crashes before they ever reach production users makes GEA one of our most important stability gates.
During the release phase, Grab uses staged rollout and feature flags to control production exposure to crashes. Staged rollout enables a new app version to reach only a small percentage of users initially, so engineers can monitor its crashes and possibly pause the rollout if an abnormal crash rate is detected. Features flags, in turn, allow teams to activate features gradually while monitoring their impact on crash rates. If a feature causes crash rates to exceed predefined thresholds, it be disabled immediately without requiring a new release.
During the post-release phase, Grab focuses on rapid incident response using mechanisms to detect, investigate, and contain production crashes. These include real-time crash monitoring using Firebase Crashlytics and BigQuery to identify anomalies as soon as a build goes live; automated triage and enriched diagnostics to aggregate crash metadata and stack traces, helping teams to map crashes to specific PRs; and feedback loops and post-mortem analysis to extend lint rules and test coverage.
There is much more to Grab's layered defense approach than can be covered here. Be sure to read the full article for all the details.

candidato.titulo: TSMC denies exploring 3D DRAM at Nvidia's request
candidato.resumo: Nvidia reportedly asks TSMC to produce '3D DRAM' to address memory shortages.

texto_fonte:
A recent report from The Information suggested that TSMC is exploring 3D DRAM production at Nvidia's request as surging demand for AI hardware strains global DRAM supplies and drives up prices. If the proposal were to come to fruition, it could mean a new, albeit prone to cyclical risks, business for TSMC and could dramatically expand its role in the AI supply chain. For its part, TSMC states that it is a pure-play logic foundry and plans to remain a logic foundry, which essentially means a denial of the report.
"Please note that TSMC focuses on our core business at all times, which is dedicated IC foundry," a TSMC spokesperson told Tom's Hardware. "Our mission is to be the trusted technology and capacity provider of the global logic IC industry for years to come."
Despite the denial, according to two people familiar with the initiative cited by The Information, TSMC has begun preparing plans for 3D DRAM manufacturing following a request from Nvidia, its largest customer. The initiative is reportedly overseen by Hsu Kuo-chin, TSMC’s vice president responsible for advanced packaging and former head of Micron’s Taiwanese operations. The effort comes amid widespread memory shortages that turned memory from a commodity into a strategic asset that could determine whether a company can ship its products to customers or not.
Although TSMC works closely with DRAM producers as it packages memory into system-in-packages (SiPs) for its customers, the company lacks the expertise and production capacity to make DRAM, let alone 3D DRAM. Meanwhile, given that 3D DRAM is years away even for major memory makers, pursuing a 3D DRAM strategy cannot solve memory shortages for at least five years.
Unlike conventional DRAM, which arranges memory cells in a single plane, 3D DRAM places multiple levels of memory cells vertically to increase capacity per wafer. All three leading DRAM makers — Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix — are working on their 3D DRAM projects. However, Micron's DRAM strategy includes at least four more planar DRAM process technologies before 3D DRAM becomes a reality.
While TSMC has arguably the industry's best logic process technologies, DRAM production requires entirely different manufacturing processes, which TSMC would have to develop, should it pursue making memory for its customers. Meanwhile, producing 3D DRAM requires completely different fabrication techniques to construct multiple memory-cell layers while controlling defects and maintaining acceptable yields. It is hardly possible to develop a 3D DRAM manufacturing process without having a competitive planar DRAM process technology, and TSMC does not have one.
One of the options for TSMC to enter the DRAM business would be to acquire a small specialty memory producer that has its own fabrication capability. This would give TSMC a credible route into advanced DRAM manufacturing without having to develop the underlying memory technology and IPs from scratch. However, small makers do not have leading-edge commodity DRAM nodes, so TSMC would still need to invest billions of dollars and years of R&D into development of a leading-edge process technology for DRAM.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
However, entering DRAM manufacturing would expose TSMC to substantial market risks. Memory shortages frequently encourage capacity expansions that eventually create oversupply, depressing prices and profitability. Such uncertainty could surely make TSMC think twice before going down the DRAM route. Furthermore, entering the DRAM business could also complicate TSMC's relationship with large DRAM makers in general, and SK Hynix, which partnered with the foundry in 2024 to manufacture logic base dies for next-generation HBM products, in particular.
TSMC’s potential entry into DRAM manufacturing could also raise antitrust questions, particularly if the company combines its dominant position in leading-edge logic manufacturing, leading position in advanced chip packaging, and ramping memory production. Regulators could examine whether such vertical integration would enable TSMC to favor its own memory products or disadvantage competitors that lack such a vertical integration. Then again, in-house DRAM development by TSMC could also strengthen competition by introducing another supplier into a market dominated by just three manufacturers.
Yet, TSMC does not necessarily need to manufacture DRAM to capitalize on growing demand for advanced memory. Instead, it could capture a larger share of the value generated by DRAM by producing sophisticated logic base dies for HBM, integrating memory with processors using its SoIC hybrid bonding technology, and developing customized memory solutions with partners such as GUC and established DRAM manufacturers. This approach would allow TSMC to expand its presence in the advanced memory market without investing billions of dollars in developing competitive DRAM process technologies from scratch and/or building additional fabs for tens of billions of dollars.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

candidato.titulo: Theory predicting an older universe without dark matter or dark energy passes key cosmological tests
candidato.resumo: An alternative model in which the universe is 26.7 billion years old and needs neither dark matter nor dark energy has held up against several major cosmology tests, according to a new University of Ottawa study. The research, titled "A Big Bang Nucleosynthesis Consistency Test of the CCC+TL Cosmology," is published in the journal Universe.

texto_fonte:
Theory predicting an older universe without dark matter or dark energy passes key cosmological tests
An alternative model in which the universe is 26.7 billion years old and needs neither dark matter nor dark energy has held up against several major cosmology tests, according to a new University of Ottawa study. The research, titled "A Big Bang Nucleosynthesis Consistency Test of the CCC+TL Cosmology," is published in the journal Universe.
One model, many observations
During 2025 and 2026, Rajendra Gupta, adjunct professor in uOttawa's Department of Physics, and postdoctoral researcher Dr. Nikolaos Samaras tested the CCC+TL model against a range of important astronomical observations.
CCC+TL stands for "covarying coupling constants plus tired light." The model suggests that what is usually attributed to dark matter and dark energy could instead come from evolving fundamental constants that govern how forces and particles interact.
Scientists have searched for dark matter and dark energy for decades, but neither has been directly detected. The standard cosmological model, known as ΛCDM, also faces questions raised by observations of surprisingly mature galaxies in the early universe.
"Most emerging models explain only a limited set of observations," Gupta says. "A new model must not conflict with the pillars of cosmology and astrophysics, and our findings meet that challenge, including the yet-to-be-published cosmic microwave background challenge."
CCC+TL changes the Einstein and Friedmann equations, which describe gravity and the expansion of the universe. That meant the researchers couldn't just modify the standard model and existing computer codes. For each test, they developed CCC+TL-compliant equations and code.
What the tests found
The model's results agreed with several major observations. Its predictions for the amounts of hydrogen, helium and other light elements formed shortly after the Big Bang matched those of the standard model. It also agreed with cosmic-chronometer measurements, which use the ages of galaxies to estimate how fast the universe has expanded over time.
In a recent paper published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, the researchers also applied the model to all 175 galaxies in the SPARC database and found it could reproduce their rotation curves without dark matter. A separate study of time dilation in supernova observations also supports the model, although that paper is still under review.
The team looked at the Bullet Cluster too. There, the extra gravitational effect the model predicts, rather than the dark matter, tracks the galaxies, not the hot, X-ray-emitting gas. The researchers call this an early proof of concept that needs more study.
"Observations attributed to dark matter and dark energy likely originate from covarying coupling constants," adds Gupta, whose paper on the origin of dark matter and dark energy explores the idea.
More time for early galaxies to form
The model could also help explain why astronomers keep finding large, mature galaxies so early in cosmic history.
In the standard model, the universe was about 300 million years old during cosmic dawn. Under CCC+TL, it would have been about 4.6 billion years old at the same observed redshift. That extra time gives galaxies longer to grow and develop. In the researchers' calculations, early galaxies come out about 12 times larger in size and mass than the standard model predicts, as reported in Galaxies.
"Impossible early galaxies become predictable galaxies," Gupta explains. "We predict that galaxies exist well beyond the distances the James Webb Space Telescope has reached."
That prediction may soon be tested. The James Webb Space Telescope's GLIMPSE program plans to search for galaxies at redshifts that may exceed 50. In the standard model, there may not be enough time for massive galaxies to form that early. CCC+TL has no such limit.
"The success should encourage astronomers to take the new model seriously. It is challenging to understand and apply, but we believe it extends the physics of the universe beyond ΛCDM limits," concludes Gupta.
Publication details
Rajendra P. Gupta et al., A Big Bang Nucleosynthesis Consistency Test of the CCC+TL Cosmology, Universe (2026). DOI: 10.3390/universe12070193

candidato.titulo: AI-Assisted Proof Settles Longstanding Question About Quantum Speedups
candidato.resumo: Insider Brief A mathematical proof has resolved a conjecture open since 2008 about when quantum computers can achieve enormous advantages over conventional machines, establishing a limit on their ability to outperform classical algorithms on unstructured inputs. The result proves the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, which connects a question about mathematical functions to whether dramatic speedups require special […]

texto_fonte:
Insider Brief
- A proof of the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture establishes that exponential quantum advantages in input reads require structure when answering yes-or-no questions on most randomly generated inputs.
- PSI said its research system used a non-public Anthropic model to find the proof, which was checked in the Lean proof assistant and reviewed by researchers.
- The theorem limits data reads rather than total computing time, leaving room for practical quantum advantages and further work to strengthen its mathematical bounds.
A mathematical proof has resolved a conjecture open since 2008 about when quantum computers can achieve enormous advantages over conventional machines, establishing a limit on their ability to outperform classical algorithms on unstructured inputs.
The result proves the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, which connects a question about mathematical functions to whether dramatic speedups require special structure in the problems being solved, a central issue in quantum computing, namely.
For quantum computing, the practical implication is a clearer direction for quantum algorithm research toward problems whose mathematical or physical structure offers an advantage. The theorem strengthens the theoretical basis for that approach, although it does not ultimately determine which applications will deliver useful speedups.
According to a paper posted on git hub by David Turturean of Physical Superintelligence, or PSI, the answer is yes within a widely used framework that measures how often an algorithm accesses its input. For yes-or-no computations, a classical algorithm can approximate a quantum algorithm’s probability of answering yes on most uniformly random inputs without needing exponentially more accesses.
PSI said in an accompanying blog post that an internally developed research system, using instances of a non-public Anthropic model, found a complete proof during the third day of a run. The paper says the main theorem and its formulation of the original conjecture were formalized in Lean, a proof assistant, and checked by its kernel, the software component that verifies the logical steps.
The Boundary Between Quantum and Classical
The finding sharpens the theoretical boundary between quantum and classical computing. It establishes a limit on how often a computer must read the data supplied to a problem, known as its input. That measure does not account for all the work needed to process the data, so the theorem does not establish a general limit on total computing time or the commercial value of quantum machines.
The conjecture takes its name from Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis, whose work connected the quantum computing question to a statement about polynomials. The new paper traces the conjecture to a 2008 lecture by Aaronson and builds on a series of results from mathematics and theoretical computer science.
One reason the question matters is that quantum computing’s best-known potential advantages exploit patterns.
Peter Shor’s factoring algorithm, introduced in 1994, uses quantum computation to find the period of a repeating mathematical function. That approach offers a route to factoring large numbers far faster than any known classical method. As PSI’s blog explains, the periodic pattern supplies structure that a quantum algorithm can exploit.
The Aaronson-Ambainis question concerns what happens when such favorable conditions are absent. Can a quantum algorithm still gain an exponential advantage when presented with a uniformly random string of zeros and ones?
The Query Model
To study that question, researchers use the query model. Instead of counting every operation a computer performs, the model counts its requests for information about an input. A classical query reads a bit at a selected position. A quantum query can act on a superposition of positions, allowing the algorithm to use interference as it processes information.
If that sounds a bit esoteric, imagine the input as a row of closed boxes, each holding a zero or a one. A classical query opens one box and reads its contents. A quantum query can interact with several boxes at once, but it does not reveal everything inside them. Instead, a quantum algorithm combines the effects of those interactions to uncover information about the collection, such as a hidden pattern.
If even that sounds a bit esoteric, it may be better to know that the framework gives researchers a precise way to compare the information each kind of machine needs. It also makes the result narrower than a claim that conventional computers can efficiently reproduce everything quantum computers do.
The paper establishes that, for a quantum algorithm making a given number of queries, there is a deterministic classical algorithm that approximates its acceptance probability — its probability of answering yes — on all but a chosen small fraction of inputs. For fixed accuracy and a fixed allowance for exceptional inputs, the classical query count grows as a fixed power of the quantum query count.
In other words, for most randomly generated inputs, a conventional computer can estimate the quantum algorithm’s probability of answering yes without needing vastly more reads of the data. The finding concerns those reads, rather than the total time needed to produce an answer.
Earlier research supplied a crucial link between quantum computing and mathematics. It showed that a quantum algorithm’s probability of answering yes can be described by a mathematical formula, with the formula’s complexity limited by how often the algorithm reads its input.
The formula translates the input data into the probability that the quantum algorithm will answer yes. It also captures how different pieces of that data work together to affect the answer.
Aaronson and Ambainis proposed that, for the mathematical formulas describing these quantum algorithms, there must be at least one piece of input data with a measurable effect on the result whenever that result varies meaningfully across inputs.
That would give a conventional computer a way to decide what information to read next. Rather than examine every bit of data, it could focus on bits that most affect the quantum algorithm’s probability of answering yes.
The method described in PSI’s blog assumes the conventional computer already knows the formula describing that probability. It reads an influential bit, updates its assessment and then selects another. Once the unread data has little effect on the prediction, it stops and estimates the probability by averaging over the remaining possibilities.
The conjecture was the missing guarantee that this process could make sufficient progress without requiring exponentially more reads of the data.
Supplying the Guarantee
Turturean’s paper supplies that guarantee. It establishes a minimum effect that at least one input bit must have, based on the complexity of the formula and how much its result varies. Crucially, adding more input bits does not, by itself, weaken the guarantee.
According to the paper, earlier mathematical results offered guarantees that became too weak as the formulas grew more complex. The new result overcomes that obstacle and establishes the relationship needed to prove the conjecture.
The proof builds on an approach developed by Shachar Lovett and Jiapeng Zhang. Their strategy examines which inputs produce results above or below a series of thresholds, providing a way to study how changes in the data affect the outcome.
A central advance is a new method of matching different arrangements of input data, according to the study. The matching follows restrictions on where the arrangements agree or differ, allowing the proof to connect changes in individual bits to the behavior of the formula as a whole. It strengthens an earlier mathematical result known as David Reimer’s Butterfly Lemma.
The paper also finds that one mathematical claim proposed by Lovett and Zhang does not hold in its stated general form. The new proof retains their broader strategy while replacing that claim with a different result.
The advance follows recent progress on a narrower version of the quantum computing question. According to PSI’s blog, Stanford University researchers Guy Blanc, Jordan Docter, Carmen Strassle and Li-Yang Tan showed in August 2026 that quantum algorithms could not achieve exponential savings in data reads on random inputs when restricted to a fixed number of rounds, with multiple reads allowed in each round.
PSI said those researchers have been reading the full proof, providing comments and preparing a shorter explanation for experts. The paper acknowledges their contributions.
That work complements the checks performed by Lean. The software verifies that the formalized proof follows its mathematical rules, while researchers can examine the reasoning, explain why it works and assess its implications.
The paper also describes how AI contributed to the discovery. Multiple instances of the Anthropic model searched existing research, proposed ideas, combined approaches and tested arguments. Some instances coordinated work among others within the research system Turturean developed.
Turturean selected and defined the problem, operated the system and prompted a model to assemble the results into a first draft. According to the paper’s disclosure, he personally reviewed and edited the draft and takes responsibility for its correctness.
The first complete proof emerged during the third day of the run, according to the paper’s discovery timeline. It settled the conjecture with a weaker guarantee than the final version.
After the model instances were directed to investigate related open problems, they twice improved the mathematical bound. The initial proof and both improvements were checked in Lean, according to the appendix.
The account documents a substantial AI-assisted discovery, although it does not establish how consistently the system could solve other longstanding problems. The model used in the run is non-public, and the work relied on a research system developed and operated by humans.
Limits and Future Work
The quantum computing result also has important limits.
It allows a conventional computer to estimate a quantum algorithm’s probability of answering yes for most randomly generated inputs, within a chosen margin of error. It does not guarantee an accurate estimate for every input or show how to reproduce every kind of quantum computation.
The result also concerns how often a computer needs to read its data. It does not account for all the work required to decide which bits to read or calculate an answer.
This might bear out in practice when a conventional computer might need relatively few reads but still perform a large amount of computation between them. The paper’s explicit guarantee also permits a substantial number of reads, particularly when a highly accurate estimate is required. Establishing that the cost avoids exponential growth does not necessarily make the method practical.
The theorem therefore leaves room for substantial quantum advantages, including more moderate speedups on unstructured inputs and dramatic gains on problems with useful structure.
As for further mathematical questions, the paper does not establish the strongest possible guarantee for how influential an input bit must be. Improving that guarantee could tighten the resulting limits on how many reads a conventional computer needs.
The manuscript also asks whether its central matching step can be achieved through a direct construction. The current proof establishes that a suitable matching exists through an algebraic argument. A direct method could make that part of the reasoning easier to understand and use.
With the conjecture resolved, researchers may take part in future research to pursue those sharper limits and investigate what the proof’s methods reveal about other problems in mathematics and computing.
Matt Swayne

candidato.titulo: US FAA to eliminate floppy disks from air traffic control by 2028
candidato.resumo: The US federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is finally moving to retire floppy disks from its air traffic control infrastructure, with plans to to replace four decades-old information systems across 435 facilities by the end of 2028.

texto_fonte:
The US federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is finally moving to retire floppy disks from its air traffic control infrastructure, with plans to replace four decades-old information systems across 435 facilities by the end of 2028. The agency announced the rollout on November 5, introducing a centralized platform that will give controllers faster access to weather reports, flight alerts and other operational information. “We’re moving away from outdated, manual processes and replacing technology that once relied on floppy disks with a modern system that allows controllers to instantly share critical flight alerts, restricted airspace schedules and pilot reports,” FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said, adding the agency wants to make critical information available more quickly across its networks.
Notably, the new Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS) is designed to replace four legacy systems dating back to the 1980s. Rather than relying on separate information displays and manual processes, controllers will get a centralized view of operational updates, equipment problems, weather disruptions, and aviation advisories. The first five locations receiving E-IDS include Atlantic City International Airport, Nashville International Airport, Greater Rochester International Airport, and FAA data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City, although the system could be extended to 453 sites by the end of 2028.
The upgrade comes amid mounting pressure on the FAA to modernize infrastructure that has become increasingly difficult to maintain. Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion for air traffic control improvements, while Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is seeking another $30 billion for additional upgrades. The agency problems extend well beyond removable storage. The FAA still relies on decades-old Company computers and replacement parts sourced from eBay. Its facilities also operate with separate systems that make information sharing more difficult, with Bedford previously saying “every facility is a silo.”
Communication failures have also exposed weaknesses in the infrastructure. Last month, the FAA sent a memo to airports warning about several recent outages caused by fiber optic cable cuts, which can trigger flight delays, diversions and, in worst cases, cancellations. One incident occurred in mid-October when a construction-related cable cut outside George Bush Intercontinental Airport disrupted data services between FAA facilities, forcing a ground stop. September also saw thousands of flights delayed or canceled across the Northeast after a circuit failure at a Philadelphia air traffic facility and in New Jersey.
That said, mission-critical infrastructure struggling to abandon obsolete systems is not entirely new. In June 2025, we covered the FAA's earlier modernization plans, which also targeted paper flight trips and computers reportedly running Windows 95. The agency has been gradually introducing electronic flight trips since the Biden era, with the transition expected to reach 49 major airports by at least 2028. So far, only 27 have made the switch. San Francisco has faced a similar challenge with its Muni Metro light rail network, with the city awarding Hitachi Rail a $212 million contract to replace its floppy-disk-based control system in 2024.
The German Navy has also been looking to replace 8-inch floppy drives used aboard its Brandenburg-class frigates. These disks are part of a data acquisition system connected to basic ship functions, including propulsion and power generation. Japan, meanwhile, finally moved the remaining government regulations requiring floppy disk submissions in June 2024, eliminating 1,034 such rules.

texto_fonte:
O que são e como funcionam os dots do ChatGPT?
Por Viviane França • Editado por Jones Oliveira |
Os dots são agentes de inteligência artificial que trabalham continuamente para executar tarefas e acompanhar projetos. Ao contrário dos chatbots, que apenas respondem a comandos, os agentes podem atuar em segundo plano, aprender preferências e assumir atividades que envolvem várias etapas.
A ferramenta faz parte de uma tendência de expansão dos agentes de IA. Com computadores próprios na nuvem, navegadores e acesso a aplicativos conectados, os dots conseguem pesquisar informações, organizar fluxos de trabalho e desenvolver projetos completos.
O recurso pode ser usado por usuários comuns e empresas. Sua proposta é delegar atividades recorrentes e trabalhos complexos para agentes, que são capazes de acompanhar as necessidades de cada pessoa ou equipe.
A seguir, confira:
- O que são dots no ChatGPT?
- Como funcionam os dots no ChatGPT?
- Tem como definir limites para os dots?
- Como criar um dot no ChatGPT?
O que são dots no ChatGPT?
Os dots são agentes de inteligência artificial que permanecem ativos e assumem tarefas de forma contínua. Cada agente conta com um computador próprio na nuvem e um navegador integrado, além de poder alternar entre os modelos avançados GPT-6 Astra e GPT-6.1 Terra, de acordo com as necessidades de cada etapa do trabalho.
Com o tempo, os dots podem aprender quais informações são importantes para o usuário, identificar suas preferências e usar esse contexto em atividades futuras. Para isso, existem dois tipos de agentes:
- Dot individual: funciona como um assistente pessoal que acompanha os objetivos e as preferências do usuário. Com acesso às memórias do ChatGPT, pode ajudar na revisão de código, produção de conteúdo, acompanhamento de métricas de vendas e pesquisa de artigos científicos.
- Dots especialistas: são focados no ambiente corporativo e têm identidade, permissões e recursos próprios. As empresas podem configurar agentes para atividades específicas, como compras, processamento de faturas, marketing por e-mail, atendimento ao cliente e contratação comercial. Eles também podem ser integrados a plataformas empresariais, como o Microsoft Agent 365.
Como funcionam os dots no ChatGPT?
Embora trabalhem na nuvem, os dots também podem acessar o computador do usuário. Para isso, é necessário autorizar o acesso pelo aplicativo do ChatGPT para desktop. Com essa permissão, o agente consegue consultar arquivos locais, usar programas instalados e navegar pela internet.
Os dots também contam com o recurso de pesquisa proativa, que mantém o agente em busca de maneiras de ajudar mesmo quando o usuário não está conversando com ele. Para isso, a IA consulta informações e acompanha atualizações dos aplicativos conectados, mas tem acesso apenas à leitura dos dados. Além disso, é possível programar tarefas e criar rotinas recorrentes. O andamento das atividades fica organizado em três seções: “Em andamento”, “Agendadas” e “Concluídas”.
Também é possível conectar o dot a mais de 4 mil aplicativos, incluindo Google Agenda, Google Drive e GitHub. Além disso, dá para conversar com o agente pela versão web, pelos aplicativos para computador e celular, por chamadas de voz e por plataformas, como Slack e Microsoft Teams.
Os dots ainda podem criar e gerenciar tarefas em ambientes do Codex e trabalhar com o ChatGPT Work. As conversas por texto ou voz com o dot também não consomem a cota tradicional de mensagens do ChatGPT. Já as tarefas executadas pelo Codex ou pelo ChatGPT Work entram nos limites de uso dessas ferramentas.
Tem como definir limites para os dots?
Mesmo com autonomia para executar tarefas, os dots seguem regras de segurança definidas pelo usuário, pela empresa ou pelo sistema. Um dos mecanismos de proteção é a Revisão Automática, que verifica se ações envolvendo contas e compartilhamento de dados respeitam as instruções configuradas. Além disso, algumas atividades são restritas e precisam de intervenção humana para serem feitas, como a alteração de senhas.
Também é possível definir o que o agente pode fazer por conta própria nas Regras Personalizadas. Há quatro níveis de permissão:
- Pode executar uma tarefa sem pedir autorização;
- Precisa solicitar aprovação antes de agir;
- Tem que perguntar como deve proceder;
- Deve transferir o controle para o usuário.
Essas instruções, porém, não anulam as proteções de segurança integradas ou liberam acessos que não foram autorizados. Mesmo que o usuário conceda permissões amplas, ações consideradas críticas continuam bloqueadas ou dependem de uma intervenção humana.
Para configurar as permissões, é só seguir o passo a passo abaixo:
- Abra o perfil do agente;
- Entre em “Personalizar”;
- Vá em “Regras Personalizadas”;
- Crie ou edite as instruções.
Depois de configurar as regras, você ainda pode intervir quando quiser. O menu de opções do perfil permite pausar o dot imediatamente, a aba de atividades mostra o andamento do trabalho e as ações executadas em segundo plano podem ser acompanhadas e auditadas em tempo real.
Como criar um dots no ChatGPT?
Para criar um dots, é necessário ter uma assinatura do ChatGPT Pro, Business Premium ou Entreprise. Depois, basta seguir os passos:
- Abra o aplicativo do ChatGPT ou acesse chatgpt.com/dots pelo navegador;
- Siga as instruções do assistente de configuração para criar o primeiro agente;
- Escolha um nome para o dot;
- Selecione um avatar para representar o agente. Também é possível solicitar a geração de uma imagem para o mascote.

texto_fonte:
Review Leapmotor C10 REEV: um SUV para enterrar qualquer preconceito
Por Paulo Amaral |
Quando o CT Auto dirigiu o Leapmotor C10 REEV pela primeira vez, uma coisa ficou clara: o SUV da marca chinesa tinha uma proposta diferente dos outros eletrificados que estavam chegando ao Brasil. Não era simplesmente mais um híbrido plug-in, nem um elétrico com uma bateria enorme. A ideia era entregar a experiência de um carro elétrico e usar um motor a combustão para resolver justamente o maior receio de quem ainda não migrou para essa tecnologia: a autonomia.
Depois de conviver novamente com o modelo, agora por um período bem maior, a proposta ficou ainda mais clara. O C10 REEV tem 215 cv, tração traseira e 32,6 kgf/m entregues pelo motor elétrico. Já o motor 1.5 a gasolina, aspirado e de ciclo Atkinson, não movimenta as rodas. Ele funciona exclusivamente como gerador para alimentar a bateria de 28,4 kWh quando necessário.
E é aí que aparece o grande trunfo do SUV. A Leapmotor declara 950 km de autonomia combinada no ciclo WLTP (111 km de autonomia elétrica no PBEV/Inmetro), enquanto a bateria pode ser recarregada de 30% a 80% em 18 minutos em carregador DC. Na prática, isso permite usar o C10 como um elétrico no dia a dia e ainda ter um “plano B” para viagens longas. Ou seja: o C10 REEV se mostrou pronto para enterrar qualquer preconceito contra eletrificados.
Prós e Contras
Prós
- Experiência de condução elétrica
- Até 950 km de autonomia combinada
- Motor elétrico de 215 cv
- Bom acerto de suspensão e direção
- Excelente espaço interno
- Acabamento acima da média
- Lista de equipamentos bastante completa
- Atualizações de sistema OTA (Over-the-Air)
Contras
- Muitos comandos básicos ficam escondidos na central
- Ausência de Android Auto e Apple CarPlay
- Motor gerador pode ficar bastante perceptível em viagens
- Porta-malas menor que o do C10 elétrico
Como anda o Leapmotor C10 REEV
A melhor qualidade do C10 REEV aparece justamente quando ele funciona como um carro elétrico de verdade. O motor traseiro entrega 215 cv e 32,6 kgf/m de forma imediata, e a resposta ao acelerador é progressiva e silenciosa. Não há troca de marcha ou qualquer interrupção na entrega de força, porque é o motor elétrico que movimenta o SUV o tempo inteiro.
O conjunto também surpreende pelo acerto dinâmico. O C10 é grande e pesado, mas não passa a sensação de ser desajeitado. A suspensão filtra bem os buracos sem deixar a carroceria excessivamente solta, enquanto a direção ganha um peso agradável no modo esportivo. O consumo homologado pelo Inmetro é de 12 km/l na cidade e 12 km/l na estrada, embora a experiência real possa variar bastante conforme o modo de funcionamento do sistema REEV.
O que não gostei no SUV da Leap
O principal problema do C10 está dentro da cabine. A Leapmotor apostou pesado em uma experiência digital, mas exagerou um pouquinho no tom e levou a ideia longe demais em alguns momentos. Praticamente tudo passa pela central Leap One de 14,6 polegadas, incluindo funções que poderiam ter comandos físicos mais simples, como o ajuste do espelho ou o travamento das portas (este também presente no volante). Até tarefas básicas exigem algum tempo de adaptação.
A ausência de Android Auto e Apple CarPlay também incomoda. A marca oferece internet embarcada, aplicativos próprios, navegador integrado e atualizações remotas, mas isso não substitui completamente o espelhamento do smartphone para quem já está acostumado com esses sistemas. A chave NFC também parece mais uma demonstração de tecnologia do que uma solução realmente prática para o cotidiano.
Tecnologias do Leapmotor C10 REEV
O pacote tecnológico é um dos pontos fortes do SUV. Além da central de 14,6 polegadas, há painel digital de 10,25 polegadas, chave digital pelo smartphone, cartão NFC, atualizações remotas, carregador de celular por indução, teto panorâmico, bancos dianteiros elétricos com aquecimento e ventilação e sistema de som de 840 W com 12 alto-falantes.
Na segurança, o Leap Pilot reúne recursos como piloto automático adaptativo, frenagem autônoma de emergência, alerta de ponto cego, alerta de tráfego cruzado traseiro, assistente de permanência em faixa (que chega a ser um pouco “chato” às vezes), leitura de placas, câmeras com visão 360 graus e sete airbags. Há ainda V2L e recarga rápida DC, que leva a bateria de 30% a 80% em 18 minutos.
A experiência elétrica é realmente boa?
A experiência ao volante do SUV da Leapmotor talvez seja o ponto mais importante para entender o C10 REEV. Ele é um carro elétrico na condução, mesmo quando o motor a combustão está ligado. O 1.5 aspirado de ciclo Atkinson não traciona as rodas em nenhum momento. Sua única função é gerar energia para a bateria e, consequentemente, para o motor elétrico.
Na cidade, isso funciona muito bem. Com a bateria carregada, o C10 entrega silêncio, suavidade e resposta imediata, exatamente como um elétrico convencional. A diferença aparece quando a carga diminui e o gerador precisa trabalhar por períodos mais longos. Nesse momento, o motorista passa a ouvir mais o 1.5, principalmente em acelerações fortes e trechos de estrada.
Vale a pena comprar o Leapmotor C10 REEV?
Para quem busca a experiência de um carro elétrico, sim, o C10 REEV faz sentido. Na verdade, essa é justamente uma das situações em que ele mais se destaca. Quem pode carregar em casa e usa o carro principalmente na cidade terá boa parte dos benefícios de um elétrico, enquanto o motor gerador elimina a preocupação de ficar procurando carregador em uma viagem inesperada. A própria Leapmotor recomenda o modo EV para uso urbano e para quem tem ponto de recarga em casa ou no trabalho.
A ressalva aparece para quem viaja muito. Em longos trechos sem recarga, o gerador passa a trabalhar com maior frequência e a experiência fica menos silenciosa. Nesse cenário, um híbrido plug-in tradicional pode ser mais interessante dependendo do perfil. Mas, se a prioridade é ter a sensação de um elétrico sem abrir mão da liberdade de abastecer em um posto, o C10 REEV entrega exatamente essa proposta. É esse equilíbrio, e não apenas os 950 km de autonomia, que faz dele um carro diferente.
E aí: curtiu o C10 REEV? Então nada melhor do que aproveitar para entender melhor sobre esse tipo de motorização, certo? Confira em detalhes o que é e como funciona um carro com a tecnologia EREV.
* A unidade do Leapmotor C10 REEV utilizada para esse review está avaliada em R$ 219.990 (em outubro de 2026) e foi gentilmente cedida ao Canaltech pela Stellantis South America.

texto_fonte:
OPPO pode cancelar celular que prometia câmera poderosa e filmagem de cinema
Por Bruno Bertonzin |
A OPPO pode cancelar o lançamento do Find X10 Ultra, celular que prometia um conjunto de câmeras poderoso, com especificações voltadas para fotografia profissional e gravações cinematográficas. Segundo um novo vazamento, a fabricante chinesa teria suspendido o desenvolvimento do aparelho, que seria o sucessor do Find X9 Ultra.
A informação foi divulgada pelo conhecido informante Digital Chat Station, em uma publicação na rede social chinesa Weibo. Apesar de não citar diretamente o nome do dispositivo na publicação inicial, o leaker esclareceu nos comentários que o modelo da atual geração teria sido cancelado.
Até o momento, a OPPO não confirmou a informação e também não explicou os possíveis motivos para a decisão. Portanto, ainda não é possível afirmar se o projeto foi definitivamente encerrado ou se a fabricante pretende retomá-lo futuramente.
OPPO Find X10 Ultra prometia câmeras de até 200 MP
O possível cancelamento chama atenção principalmente pelas especificações fotográficas esperadas para o celular. Um vazamento divulgado nesta semana indicou que o Find X10 Ultra poderia contar com três câmeras de 200 MP e uma quarta de 50 MP.
O conjunto seria composto por um sensor principal de 200 MP, uma ultrawide de 200 MP e uma câmera telefoto periscópica de 200 MP com zoom óptico de 3 vezes. Para completar, o aparelho teria outra telefoto periscópica de 50 MP, com aproximação óptica de 10 vezes.
Essa configuração colocaria o dispositivo entre os celulares mais avançados para fotografia, especialmente pela versatilidade das lentes e pela possibilidade de capturar imagens com alto nível de detalhes em diferentes distâncias.
O aparelho também criava expectativas para gravações de vídeo com qualidade cinematográfica, embora os rumores ainda não tenham detalhado quais recursos específicos seriam oferecidos nesse sentido.
Por que a OPPO pode cancelar o Find X10 Ultra?
Ainda não há informações concretas sobre o motivo da possível suspensão. Uma das hipóteses levantadas é o aumento dos custos de componentes, especialmente das memórias RAM, que enfrentam uma crise de preços no mercado global.
No entanto, não há qualquer confirmação de que esse cenário tenha influenciado a decisão da OPPO.
O Find X9 Ultra foi lançado em maio de 2026, portanto, seu sucessor ainda não era esperado para os próximos meses. Isso significa que a fabricante teria tempo para rever o projeto antes de um eventual anúncio oficial.
Por enquanto, o futuro do Find X10 Ultra permanece incerto. A OPPO não divulgou um posicionamento sobre os rumores nem confirmou se pretende manter a linha Ultra em sua próxima geração de smartphones.
